Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This large analysis gives a defensible framework for talking about borderline amyloid PET quantitation. It does not replace expert visual interpretation and showed substantial between-study heterogeneity. A blood, CSF, or repeat imaging result may be useful when quantitation and visual read disagree.

Study design

Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 49,227 scans from 53 studies and five tracers in 15 countries. Gaussian mixture and visual-read correspondence methods were analyzed separately.

Key quantitative results

  • Data-driven single positivity cutoff: 18 Centiloids (95% CI, 16â€“19; IÂ²=97%).
  • Double cutoff: <11 high-confidence negative (95% CI, 9â€“13) and >26 high-confidence positive (24â€“28); IÂ²=95% for both.
  • Visual-read correspondence in 35,045 scans produced a 27-Centiloid cutoff (95% CI, 24â€“30) and Îº=0.86 (0.83â€“0.89).
  • The intermediate range was 11â€“26 Centiloids.

What changed

The field gained pooled quantitative benchmarks and an explicit indeterminate interval rather than another single-study threshold.

Strength of evidence

Strong quantitative synthesis with high heterogeneity and no single harmonized visual-read protocol.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Borderline Centiloid values should be treated as uncertainty, especially when used for diagnosis or treatment eligibility.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to interpreting bloodâ€“PET discordance and to explaining why a binary threshold may not reflect the uncertainty near the decision boundary.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Defines uncertainty in a common reference used for blood-assay validation; discordance may reflect PET threshold choice rather than blood-assay error alone.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Clarifying intermediate scans may require additional testing; no cost analysis was performed.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can 18 Centiloids be used as the universal positive cutoff?
No. It is a meta-estimate with high heterogeneity; method, tracer, visual read, and intended use matter.
Should quantitation override the visual read?
No. The authors state that expert visual assessment remains crucial.
What should happen in the 11â€“26 range?
Review scan quality and visual interpretation and consider another validated biomarker when uncertainty would change management.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • High between-study heterogeneity
  • No harmonized visual-read protocol
  • Limited representation from several world regions
  • Not a randomized clinical utility study

Important new evidenceâ€¢Peer-reviewed cross-sectional secondary biomarker analysisâ€¢July 1, 2026

PET, CSF, and plasma discordance was modeled as probability, not test error

In 320 ADNI participants, PET and CSF classifications disagreed in 12% even when obtained within seven days; a latent-class model used plasma AÎ²42/40 or %p-tau217 to refine uncertainty rather than declaring either PET or CSF an infallible reference.

Key quantitative results: PET-CSF discordance occurred in 12 of 98 participants tested within seven days (12%; 95% CI, 7%-20%).

BiomarkersBloodAmyloidAÎ²42/AÎ²40Biological confirmation

Added October 14, 2026 Â· DOI:10.1038/s44400-026-00109-4

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Diagnostic accuracy depends on what is treated as truth. The analysis found clinically meaningful PET-CSF disagreement even with close timing and showed how plasma can refine, but not erase, uncertainty. Sparse discordant cells and model assumptions limit direct clinical use.

Study design

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of one prespecified PET-anchored PET-CSF-plasma triad per ADNI participant (n=320). Bayesian latent-class models estimated amyloid probability from PET, CSF, and plasma AÎ²42/40 or %p-tau217, with sensitivity analyses for timing, CSF cutoffs, and PET-CSF conditional dependence.

Key quantitative results

  • PET-CSF discordance occurred in 12 of 98 participants tested within seven days (12%; 95% CI, 7%-20%).
  • Concordant PET-positive/CSF-positive and PET-negative/CSF-negative patterns mapped to posterior probabilities near 1 and 0, respectively.
  • Discordant patterns produced intermediate, often wide probabilities that shifted with plasma strata and dependence assumptions.
  • The primary Elecsys CSF AÎ²42/40 analysis was available in 138 of 320 participants, and several discordant three-test cells were sparse or unobserved.

What changed

The paper reframed multi-modality disagreement as an explicit uncertainty problem and demonstrated a way to avoid forcing every discordant result into a false-positive or false-negative label.

Strength of evidence

Exploratory methodological evidence using a well-characterized research cohort and prespecified sensitivity analyses. Clinical transportability is limited by selected ADNI participants, incomplete CSF-ratio data, sparse discordant patterns, and model assumptions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

When PET, CSF, and plasma disagree, interpretation should consider biology, timing, cutoffs, prevalence, and uncertainty rather than assuming a single modality is always correct.

Field medical relevance

Useful for questions about discordant blood, CSF, and PET results; comparator choice in validation studies; and the limits of single-reference sensitivity and specificity claims.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The work highlights reference-standard dependence: apparent blood-test errors can reflect PET-CSF biological or threshold discordance. It supports reporting uncertainty around discordant patterns rather than oversimplifying one comparator as ground truth.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The framework could eventually reduce unnecessary repeat testing in discordant cases, but it did not evaluate utilization, costs, coverage, or access.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does plasma resolve every PET-CSF disagreement?
No. It refined probabilities, but discordant patterns remained uncertain and some cells had very small samples.
Is PET the gold standard in this model?
No. PET, CSF, and plasma were treated as imperfect indicators of a latent amyloid state.
Can the posterior probabilities be used clinically now?
No. The authors framed this as an interpretive research approach, not a validated routine-care decision tool.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • ADNI research cohort
  • Only 138 participants had the primary CSF AÎ²42/40 measure
  • Sparse discordant pattern cells
  • Dependence and identifiability assumptions
  • No prospective clinical utility evaluation

Primary source Â· DOI

Verma K, Kumar S. Amyloid probability in Alzheimer disease from plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and amyloid imaging. npj Dement. 2026;2:49. doi:10.1038/s44400-026-00109-4.

BiomarkersTau PETTau tanglesAmyloidDisease staging

Added September 4, 2026 Â· DOI:10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00417-4

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is the kind of comparison that supports a relative performance statement: both tracers were used in the same participants within 45 days. Detection differences could alter staging and trial eligibility. The study did not use autopsy as a universal truth standard and does not make the tracers interchangeable.

Study design

Prospective, nonrandomized, cross-sectional study at eight North American sites; 775 enrolled and 682 completed paired tau PET, amyloid PET, and cognitive assessment within 45 days.

Key quantitative results

  • AUC for AD-related cognitive impairment was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.89â€“0.95) for MK-6240 versus 0.86 (0.75â€“0.91) for flortaucipir; P<0.0001.
  • Neocortical tau positivity in cognitively impaired participants was 28% with MK-6240 versus 16% with flortaucipir.
  • Among AÎ²-positive participants, the prevalence ratio was 1.74 (95% CI, 1.32â€“2.29).
  • Regional positivity was concordant in 87% for medial temporal and 94% for neocortical classifications.

What changed

The largest paired comparison showed that tracer selection is not a neutral technical detail, particularly for earlier and neocortical tau detection.

Strength of evidence

Strong comparative clinical-validity evidence for the studied imaging definitions; clinical-outcome utility and autopsy accuracy were not primary endpoints.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Tau PET reports and trial criteria should identify the tracer and threshold. Results from one tracer should not be assumed equivalent to another.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions about why the same patient might stage differently by tracer and whether newer tau PET can refine anti-amyloid or anti-tau trial selection.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Not a blood-assay study, but it affects the imaging reference standard used to validate blood biomarkers and define discordance.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Tracer distribution, reader training, and PET capacity may determine real-world availability; no payer or cost comparison was tested.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was this a true head-to-head comparison?
Yes. Participants received both tau tracers within 45 days, with the same amyloid and cognitive context.
Does more positive mean more accurate?
Not automatically. Greater detection and discrimination were shown, but the reference framework was not universal autopsy confirmation.
Can studies using the two tracers be pooled directly?
Not without tracer-specific harmonization; their binding and dynamic ranges differ.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Nonrandomized
  • 93% of participants identified as White
  • No universal neuropathology reference
  • Cross-sectional primary comparison
  • Sponsor relationships disclosed

Povala G, Bellaver B, Lussier FZ, et al; HEAD Study. Comparison of [18F]flortaucipir and [18F]MK6240 for the detection of tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease. Lancet. Published online May 28, 2026. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00417-4.

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is a legitimate same-population comparison: identical samples, both PET modalities, and three platforms. Ella and Lumipulse had higher amyloid-PET AUCs than Simoa in this cohort, while Simoa had the lowest analytical detection range. The result illustrates why analytical sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy are different constructs.

Study design

Cross-sectional study of 113 participants (55 AD-continuum, 36 controls, 22 non-AD disorders), all with amyloid and tau PET. Cutoffs were derived in the study using Youden or two-cutoff methods.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid-PET AUC: Simoa 0.909 (95% CI, 0.846â€“0.973), Ella 0.974 (0.945â€“1.000), Lumipulse 0.965 (0.926â€“1.000).
  • Ella vs Simoa P=0.009; Lumipulse vs Simoa P=0.019; Ella vs Lumipulse P=0.294.
  • At derived single cutoffs, sensitivity/specificity were 90.9%/87.9% for Simoa, 92.7%/96.6% for Ella, and 94.6%/94.8% for Lumipulse.
  • Tau-PET AUCs were 0.937, 0.989, and 0.985, respectively.

What changed

A direct comparison quantified platform differences without relying on cross-study AUC comparisons.

Strength of evidence

Moderate for a controlled head-to-head signal; low for general platform selection because the cohort was small and cutoffs were not externally validated.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The data do not establish one universally superior assay. Platform-specific cutoffs, intended use, workflow, and external validation remain decisive.

Field medical relevance

A strong example for explaining why lower LLOQ does not automatically yield better clinical classification and why only same-cohort comparisons support relative claims.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Directly relevant to Simoa, Ella, and Lumipulse; supports precise, bounded comparison rather than broad marketing claims.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No cost, coverage, turnaround-time, or capacity comparison was performed.

Study design

Stage 1 multicenter study with a 257-person CSF-referenced derivation cohort and an independent 76-person amyloid-PET validation cohort. Dual cutoffs targeted high sensitivity and specificity.

Key quantitative results

  • CSF-referenced AUC: 0.947 for Lumipulse and 0.940 for ALZpath.

The study supplied an independent PET test of CSF-derived cutoffs and quantified the tradeoff between confident classification and the size of the intermediate zone.

Moderate: multicenter and independent validation, with small PET sample and wide predictive-value intervals.

Clinical significance

The results support a triage pathway with an explicit plan for intermediate results, not automatic substitution for PET or CSF.

Direct Simoaâ€“Lumipulse evidence in one development program; analytical sensitivity should not be equated with clinical accuracy.

Was the ratio clearly superior to p-tau217?
It reduced the indeterminate proportion in the same samples. The close AUCs should not be interpreted as universal assay superiority.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center cohort
  • Small PET subgroup
  • Mixed CSF and PET reference standard
  • Thresholds derived rather than externally prespecified
  • Industry relationships and support were reported

FDA cleared Elecsys pTau181 Plasma as a primary-care rule-out aid

At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, the single 0.722 pg/mL cutoff produced 92.7% positive agreement, 51.3% negative agreement, 97.9% NPV, and 22.4% PPV in 312 primary-care patients.

Key label details: At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%â€“97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%â€“57.2%).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau181Rule-out triage

Added October 20, 2026 Â· FDA 510(k) K252163

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The clearance is intentionally asymmetric. A negative result is consistent with a negative amyloid PET and may reduce unnecessary imaging, but nearly half of PET-negative participants tested positive. The FDA summary therefore supports rule-out triage, not standalone confirmation, and shows how low prevalence drives high NPV and low PPV.

Study design

FDA reviewed analytical validation and a pivotal clinical study in 312 evaluable primary-care patients aged at least 55 years who presented with cognitive concerns or impairment. The plasma result at a prespecified 0.722 pg/mL cutoff was compared with majority visual amyloid-PET classification; 41/312 participants were PET positive.

Key label details

  • At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%â€“97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%â€“57.2%).
  • At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, NPV was 97.9% (139/142; 95% CI, 94.0%â€“99.3%) and PPV was 22.4% (38/170; 95% CI, 19.5%â€“25.0%).
  • Three of 41 PET-positive patients tested negative, while 132 of 271 PET-negative patients tested positive.
  • FDA estimated that negative testing could reduce unnecessary amyloid PET by 45.5% (142/312).
  • The measuring range was 0.300â€“50.00 pg/mL; no high-dose hook effect was observed through 150 pg/mL.

What changed

This historical criteria-repair entry documents a previously unbriefed FDA-cleared automated p-tau181 rule-out assay and its markedly prevalence-dependent predictive values.

Strength of evidence

High regulatory and analytical-validity evidence with public pivotal performance data. Clinical utility is limited to the cleared initial-assessment aid; prospective patient-outcome benefit, specialty-care use, prognosis, and serial monitoring were not established.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A negative result can support ruling out amyloid pathology in primary care, but a positive result cannot confirm amyloid pathology and should trigger further evaluation. The intended population and low-prevalence setting are integral to interpretation.

Field medical relevance

Provides a concrete comparison point for p-tau217 assays and illustrates why intended use, cutoff architecture, prevalence, PPV, NPV, and referral setting must be separated when discussing blood tests.

Quanterix or platform relevance

This is a fully automated electrochemiluminescence assay with an 18-minute run time and a single negative/positive cutoff. Its intended role differs from three-zone p-tau217 workflows: the high NPV supports rule-out in low-prevalence primary care, while the low PPV means positive results need further investigation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA clearance establishes authorization, not universal laboratory availability, payer coverage, reimbursement, or guideline endorsement. Local ordering and payment require separate verification.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can a positive result confirm Alzheimer disease?
No. PPV was 22.4% in the pivotal primary-care cohort, and the FDA labeling says positive results should be investigated further.
Can the assay be used in specialty clinics?
Its cleared intended use is initial assessment, and the summary states it is not recommended for patients already referred to a specialist.
Can it monitor therapy or predict dementia?
No. Those uses were not established in the cleared labeling.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly source-dated development
  • Low amyloid prevalence produced very low PPV
  • Single binary cutoff leaves many false-positive results
  • Intended use is limited to initial assessment outside specialty care
  • No prognostic, treatment-monitoring, or patient-outcome utility claim
